claim: Out of 34 mutants in npr genes that were not previously linked to the control immunity, only animals lacking NPR-15 (npr-15(tm12539) and npr-15(ok1626) null animals) exhibited enhanced survival against Pseudomonas aeruginosa-mediated killing compared to wild-type (WT) animals.
source: Out of 34 mutants in npr genes that were not previously linked to the control immunity (Supplementary file 1A), only animals lacking NPR-15 (npr-15(tm12539) and npr-15(ok1626) null animals) exhibited enhanced survival against Pseudomonas aeruginosa-mediated killing compared to wild-type (WT) animals (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental survival data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and screening data in Supplementary file 1A and 1B.

claim: npr-15(tm12539) animals exhibited less visible bacterial colonization and significantly reduced colony-forming units compared to WT animals.
source: Furthermore, we found that the npr-15(tm12539) animals exhibited less visible bacterial colonization and significantly reduced colony-forming units compared to WT animals (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging data in Figure 1B and CFU quantification data in Figure 1C.

claim: The enhanced resistance to pathogen of npr-15(ok1626) animals appears to be universal, as the mutants were also found to be resistant to additional human pathogens, including Gram-negative Salmonella enterica strain 1344 and Gram-positive Enterococcus faecalis strain OG1RF and Staphylococcus aureus strain NCTCB325.
source: The enhanced resistance to pathogen of npr-15(ok1626) animals appears to be universal, as the mutants were also found to be resistant to additional human pathogens, including Gram-negative Salmonella enterica strain 1344 and Gram-positive Enterococcus faecalis strain OG1RF and Staphylococcus aureus strain NCTCB325 (Figure 1D–F)
evidence: Supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1D-F with multiple bacterial pathogens.

claim: NPR-15 suppresses defense against bacterial pathogens in general.
source: The enhanced resistance to pathogen of npr-15(ok1626) animals appears to be universal, as the mutants were also found to be resistant to additional human pathogens, including Gram-negative Salmonella enterica strain 1344 and Gram-positive Enterococcus faecalis strain OG1RF and Staphylococcus aureus strain NCTCB325 (Figure 1D–F), suggesting that NPR-15 suppresses defense against bacterial pathogens in general.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that npr-15 mutants show resistance to multiple bacterial pathogens (both Gram-negative and Gram-positive).

claim: When exposed to live Escherichia coli, the primary food source of C. elegans in the laboratory, npr-15(tm12539) animals exhibited increased lifespan compared to WT animals.
source: When exposed to live Escherichia coli, the primary food source of C. elegans in the laboratory, npr-15(tm12539) animals exhibited increased lifespan compared to WT animals (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There were no significant differences in longevity between npr-15(tm12539) and WT animals when they were exposed to lawns of E. coli that were rendered non-proliferating by ultraviolet light (UV) treatment.
source: However, there were no significant differences in longevity between npr-15(tm12539) and WT animals when they were exposed to lawns of E. coli that were rendered non-proliferating by ultraviolet light (UV) treatment (Garigan et al., 2002, Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1H and cited methodology from Garigan et al., 2002.

claim: Expression of npr-15 under the control of its own promoter rescued the enhanced survival of npr-15(tm12539) animals to different bacterial pathogens.
source: Expression of npr-15 under the control of its own promoter rescued the enhanced survival of npr-15(tm12539) animals to different bacterial pathogens (Figure 1A–G)
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1A-G.

claim: The functional loss of NPR-15 enhanced the animal's survival against live bacteria.
source: Expression of npr-15 under the control of its own promoter rescued the enhanced survival of npr-15(tm12539) animals to different bacterial pathogens (Figure 1A–G), indicating that the functional loss of NPR-15 enhanced the animal's survival against live bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing that restoring NPR-15 function reverses the enhanced survival phenotype.

claim: C. elegans exhibits avoidance behavior when encountering certain pathogenic bacteria.
source: Considering that C. elegans exhibits avoidance behavior when encountering certain pathogenic bacteria (Meisel and Kim, 2014; Chang et al., 2011; Reddy et al., 2011; Singh and Aballay, 2019a)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: npr-15(tm12539) exhibited significantly reduced pathogen avoidance when exposed to S. aureus.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that npr-15(tm12539) exhibited significantly reduced pathogen avoidance when exposed to S. aureus (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: There were no differences in re-occupancy of the lawn between WT and npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: We also compared the re-occupancy of the lawn exhibited by WT and npr-15(tm12539) animals and found no differences in their re-occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by re-occupancy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The variation in lawn occupancy is greater in WT than in npr-15(tm12539) animals across experiments.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that the variation in lawn occupancy is greater in WT than in npr-15(tm12539) animals across experiments (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The strong lack of avoidance of npr-15(tm12539) somehow counteracts the experimental variation.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that the variation in lawn occupancy is greater in WT than in npr-15(tm12539) animals across experiments (Supplementary file 2), which suggests that the strong lack of avoidance of npr-15(tm12539) somehow counteracts the experimental variation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced variation in npr-15(tm12539) animals.

claim: npr-15(tm12539) exhibited reduced learned avoidance compared to WT animals.
source: We also found that npr-15(tm12539) exhibited reduced learned avoidance compared to WT animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by learned avoidance data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Exposure to 8% oxygen to npr-15(tm12539) animals did not rescue the lack of avoidance to S. aureus.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, exposure to 8% oxygen to npr-15(tm12539) animals did not rescue the lack of avoidance to S. aureus, although it did rescue the lack of avoidance of npr-1 mutants.
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data at different oxygen levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Exposure to 8% oxygen rescued the lack of avoidance of npr-1 mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, exposure to 8% oxygen to npr-15(tm12539) animals did not rescue the lack of avoidance to S. aureus, although it did rescue the lack of avoidance of npr-1 mutants.
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data at different oxygen levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The survival of npr-15(tm12539) animals on full-lawn assays, where agar plates were completely covered by pathogenic bacteria to eliminate the possibility of pathogen avoidance, was significantly higher than that of WT animals.
source: Moreover, the survival of npr-15(tm12539) animals on full-lawn assays, where agar plates were completely covered by pathogenic bacteria to eliminate the possibility of pathogen avoidance, was significantly higher than that of WT animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by full-lawn survival assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: NPR-15 suppresses pathogen resistance and enhances avoidance behavior in response to pathogen infection, independently of oxygen concentrations.
source: These findings suggest that NPR-15 suppresses pathogen resistance and enhances avoidance behavior in response to pathogen infection, independently of oxygen concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that oxygen levels do not affect the npr-15 phenotype.

claim: C. elegans pharyngeal pumping directly affects bacterial intake.
source: Because C. elegans pharyngeal pumping directly affects bacterial intake (Styer et al., 2008; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Cao et al., 2017; Sellegounder et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: npr-15(tm12539) animals exhibited pumping rates comparable to that of WT animals.
source: We found that npr-15(tm12539) animals exhibited pumping rates comparable to that of WT animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Supported by pharyngeal pumping rate data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The dose of pathogens is similar in both npr-15(tm12539) and WT animals.
source: We found that npr-15(tm12539) animals exhibited pumping rates comparable to that of WT animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), indicating that the dose of pathogens is similar in both cases.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pumping rates are similar between mutant and WT.

claim: Bacterial accumulation in animals defective in the defecation motor program causes intestinal distension that elicits a robust immune response.
source: Moreover, it has recently been demonstrated that bacterial accumulation in animals defective in the defecation motor program causes intestinal distension that elicits a robust immune response (Singh and Aballay, 2019a)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bacterial accumulation in animals defective in the defecation motor program modulates pathogen avoidance.
source: Moreover, it has recently been demonstrated that bacterial accumulation in animals defective in the defecation motor program causes intestinal distension that elicits a robust immune response (Singh and Aballay, 2019a) and modulates pathogen avoidance (Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Singh and Aballay, 2019b; Filipowicz et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The defecation cycle of npr-15(tm12539) animals is indistinguishable from that of WT animals.
source: However, we found that the defecation cycle of npr-15(tm12539) animals is indistinguishable from that of WT animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by defecation cycle data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: NPR-15 loss-of-function enhances pathogen resistance and inhibits avoidance behavior.
source: Taken together, our results show that NPR-15 loss-of-function enhances pathogen resistance and inhibits avoidance behavior
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing enhanced survival and reduced avoidance in npr-15 mutants.

claim: NPR-15 suppresses molecular immunity while activating behavioral immunity.
source: Taken together, our results show that NPR-15 loss-of-function enhances pathogen resistance and inhibits avoidance behavior, suggesting NPR-15 suppresses molecular immunity while activating behavioral immunity.
evidence: Inferred from the dual phenotype of npr-15 mutants showing enhanced resistance but reduced avoidance.

claim: The study revealed 10 ontology clusters with high enrichment scores of vital biological functions for upregulated and downregulated genes in npr-15(tm12539).
source: The study revealed 10 ontology clusters with high enrichment scores of vital biological functions for upregulated and downregulated genes in npr-15(tm12539) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gene expression data showed significant upregulation of immune/defense response and neuropeptide signaling pathway genes in npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Overall, the gene expression data showed significant upregulation of immune/defense response and neuropeptide signaling pathway genes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Genes associated with synaptic signaling, ligand-gated channel activity, lipid metabolism, and response to biotic stimuli were also upregulated in npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Genes associated with synaptic signaling, ligand-gated channel activity, lipid metabolism, and response to biotic stimuli were also upregulated in npr-15(tm12539) animals.
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data.

claim: The analysis revealed a high enrichment of pathways crucial for C. elegans defense against bacterial infections, including the ELT-2, HLH-30, PMK-1, and DAF-2/DAF-16 insulin pathways.
source: Our analysis revealed a high enrichment of pathways crucial for C. elegans defense against bacterial infections, including the ELT-2, HLH-30, PMK-1, and DAF-2/DAF-16 insulin pathways (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4, Kerry et al., 2006; Shapira et al., 2006; Visvikis et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2002; Aballay et al., 2003; Garsin et al., 2003; Hsu et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2003; Huffman et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4, and citations to prior research.

claim: Several of the PMK-1-, HLH-30-, and DAF-16-dependent genes were also controlled by ELT-2.
source: Notably, we observed that several of the PMK-1-, HLH-30-, and DAF-16-dependent genes were also controlled by ELT-2 (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ELT-2-dependent genes play a potentially major role in the enhanced resistance to the pathogen phenotype of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Notably, we observed that several of the PMK-1-, HLH-30-, and DAF-16-dependent genes were also controlled by ELT-2 (Figure 2D), suggesting a potentially major role of ELT-2-dependent genes in the enhanced resistance to the pathogen phenotype of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ELT-2 controls many genes also controlled by other immune regulators.

claim: Quantitative PCR confirmed the upregulation of ELT-2-dependent immune genes such as dct-17, C29F3.7, T19D12.4, C32H11.4, C34H4.1, and clec-86.
source: To validate these findings, we performed quantitative PCR and confirmed the upregulation of ELT-2-dependent immune genes such as dct-17, C29F3.7, T19D12.4, C32H11.4, C34H4.1, and clec-86 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: HLH-30-dependent genes T21F4.1, argn-1, F53A9.8, and pnp-1 were validated by quantitative PCR.
source: We also validated HLH-30-dependent genes T21F4.1, argn-1, F53A9.8, and pnp-1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: NPR-15 primarily regulates C. elegans defense against bacterial infections by inhibiting immune genes, several of which are controlled by ELT-2, HLH-30, and PMK-1.
source: These transcriptomic and gene analyses indicate that NPR-15 primarily regulates C. elegans defense against bacterial infections by inhibiting immune genes, several of which are controlled by ELT-2, HLH-30, and PMK-1.
evidence: Inferred from transcriptomic and gene expression validation data.

claim: elt-2 RNAi completely suppressed the enhanced resistance to S. aureus infection in npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: We found that elt-2 RNAi completely suppressed the enhanced resistance to S. aureus infection in npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Partial suppression of pathogen resistance in npr-15(tm12539) animals was observed with hlh-30 RNAi.
source: Partial suppression of pathogen resistance in npr-15(tm12539) animals was observed with hlh-30 RNAi (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When both hlh-30 and elt-2 were inactivated in npr-15(tm12539) animals and were exposed to S. aureus, their susceptibility to infection was comparable to that of elt-2 RNAi animals.
source: Furthermore, when both hlh-30 and elt-2 were inactivated in npr-15(tm12539) animals and were exposed to S. aureus, their susceptibility to infection was comparable to that of elt-2 RNAi animals (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: pmk-1, daf-16 RNAi failed to suppress the pathogen resistance of npr-15(tm12539).
source: However, pmk-1, daf-16 RNAi failed to suppress the pathogen resistance of npr-15(tm12539) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: hlh-30 or pmk-1 mutation partly suppressed the resistance to P. aeruginosa infection phenotype of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: We found that hlh-30 or pmk-1 mutation partly suppressed the resistance to P. aeruginosa infection phenotype of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: NPR-15 suppresses ELT-2- and HLH-30-dependent molecular immunity.
source: These results indicate that NPR-15 suppresses ELT-2- and HLH-30-dependent molecular immunity.
evidence: Inferred from RNAi and genetic epistasis experiments showing that elt-2 and hlh-30 are required for the enhanced resistance phenotype of npr-15 mutants.

claim: NPR-15 is expressed in six sensory neuronal cells (ASG, ASI, ASJ, ASE, AFD, and AWC) as well as an interneuron, AVK.
source: Because NPR-15 is expressed in six sensory neuronal cells (ASG, ASI, ASJ, ASE, AFD, and AWC) as well as an interneuron, AVK (Figure 4A, Harris et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Harris et al., 2020.

claim: There are well-established synaptic connections between all the NPR-15-expressing sensory neurons.
source: First, we examined the neuronal connectome and communication between the NPR-15-expressing cell and found well-established synaptic connections between all the sensory neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by neuronal connectome data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neural-specific RNAi (strain TU3401) of NPR-15 resulted in a pathogen resistance phenotype similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Unlike intestine-specific RNAi (strain MGH171) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), neural-specific RNAi (strain TU3401) of NPR-15 resulted in a pathogen resistance phenotype similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by tissue-specific RNAi survival assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pan-neuronal promoter-driven expression of NPR-15 rescued the enhanced survival phenotype of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: This finding was further supported by rescuing NPR-15 under the control of a pan-neuronal promoter and exposing the animals to S. aureus. The results demonstrated that pan-neuronal promoter-driven expression of NPR-15 rescued the enhanced survival phenotype of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NPR-15 suppresses immunity through the nervous system.
source: These results suggest that NPR-15 suppresses immunity through the nervous system.
evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific RNAi and rescue experiments showing neuronal requirement.

claim: ASJ(-) animals exhibited resistance to pathogen-mediated killing similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: We found that ASJ(-) animals exhibited resistance to pathogen-mediated killing similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by survival assay data with neuron-ablated strains shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ASG(-) and ASE(-) neuron-ablated strains demonstrated pathogen resistance phenotype, but there is a significant difference compared to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Although the ASG(-) and ASE(-) neuron-ablated strains demonstrated pathogen resistance phenotype, there is a significant difference compared to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by survival assay data with neuron-ablated strains shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: ASJ-specific rescue of NPR-15 successfully blocked the enhanced survival of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Hence, we further confirmed the role of NPR-15/ASJ neurons in suppressing immunity by rescuing NPR-15 on ASJ unique promoter and performing survival experiments with the rescued strain. Results showed that the ASJ-specific rescue of NPR-15 successfully blocked the enhanced survival of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by ASJ-specific rescue survival data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Immune genes were upregulated in ASJ(-) animals.
source: We also quantified the expression of immune genes and found that they were upregulated in ASJ(-) animals (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: NPR-15 controls immunity in a manner similar to that of ASJ neurons.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that NPR-15 controls immunity in a manner similar to that of ASJ neurons.
evidence: Inferred from neuron ablation, rescue experiments, and gene expression data showing ASJ neuron involvement.

claim: None of the tested immune regulators (elt-2, pmk-1, daf-16, and hlh-30) were able to suppress the lack of pathogen avoidance behavior observed in response to S. aureus.
source: Our results indicate that none of the tested immune regulators (elt-2, pmk-1, daf-16, and hlh-30) were able to suppress the lack of pathogen avoidance behavior observed in response to S. aureus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data with RNAi of immune regulators shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: None of the inactivated immune genes that are not controlled by the immune regulators tested were able to suppress the lack of avoidance behavior in the npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Furthermore, we inactivated immune genes that are not controlled by the immune regulators tested above, but none of them were able to suppress the lack of avoidance behavior in the npr-15(tm12539) animals (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by RNAi screening data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The avoidance behavior observed in npr-15(tm12539) is independent of individual immune genes upregulated in npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: These findings indicate that the avoidance behavior observed in npr-15(tm12539) is independent of individual immune genes upregulated in npr-15(tm12539) animals.
evidence: Inferred from RNAi experiments showing that immune gene inactivation does not affect avoidance behavior.

claim: Neuropeptides expressed in the intestine can modulate avoidance behavior.
source: Additionally, previous studies have shown that neuropeptides expressed in the intestine can modulate avoidance behavior (Lee and Mylonakis, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Neuropeptides are among the most highly upregulated genes in npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Additionally, previous studies have shown that neuropeptides expressed in the intestine can modulate avoidance behavior (Lee and Mylonakis, 2017), and we found that neuropeptides are among the most highly upregulated genes in npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 6.

claim: None of the inactivated intestinal-expressed neuropeptides were able to suppress the lack of avoidance behavior of npr-15(tm12539) animals in response to S. aureus.
source: Our experiments revealed that none of the inactivated intestinal-expressed neuropeptides were able to suppress the lack of avoidance behavior of npr-15(tm12539) animals in response to S. aureus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by RNAi screening data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and Supplementary file 5.

claim: The absence of avoidance behavior by loss of NPR-15 function is independent of both immune and intestinal neuropeptide signaling pathways.
source: Therefore, it can be concluded that the absence of avoidance behavior by loss of NPR-15 function is independent of both immune and intestinal neuropeptide signaling pathways.
evidence: Inferred from RNAi experiments showing that neither immune genes nor neuropeptides affect avoidance behavior in npr-15 mutants.

claim: Pan-neuronal rescued strain of NPR-15 successfully rescued the suppressed pathogen avoidance of npr-15(tm12539) animal.
source: First, we investigated the avoidance behavior of a pan-neuronal rescued strain of NPR-15, which successfully rescued the suppressed pathogen avoidance of npr-15(tm12539) animal (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data with pan-neuronal rescue shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Only ASJ(-) exhibited reduced pathogen avoidance similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, we found that only ASJ(-) exhibited reduced pathogen avoidance similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data with neuron-ablated strains shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Rescuing NPR-15 under the control of an ASJ unique promoter confirmed the role of ASJ in pathogen avoidance.
source: This observation was further confirmed by rescuing NPR-15 under the control of an ASJ unique promoter (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by ASJ-specific rescue lawn occupancy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The pathogen avoidance of other neuronal-ablated strains was comparable to that of WT animals.
source: The pathogen avoidance of other neuronal-ablated strains was comparable to that of WT animals (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data with various neuron-ablated strains shown in Figure 5D-G.

claim: The loss of NPR-15 function suppresses behavioral immunity via sensory neurons, specifically ASJ.
source: These results suggest that the loss of NPR-15 function suppresses behavioral immunity via sensory neurons, specifically ASJ.
evidence: Inferred from neuron ablation and rescue experiments showing ASJ-specific requirement for avoidance behavior.

claim: TRPM ion channels, GON-2 and GTL-2, are required for pathogen avoidance.
source: Because TRPM ion channels, GON-2 and GTL-2, are required for pathogen avoidance (Filipowicz et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Only gon-2 null animals, but not gtl-2, exhibited pathogen avoidance behavior similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Our findings showed that only gon-2 null animals, but not gtl-2, exhibited pathogen avoidance behavior similar to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data with gon-2 and gtl-2 RNAi shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Both NPR-15 and GON-2 may function in a shared pathway to regulated pathogen avoidance behavior.
source: This suggests that both NPR-15 and GON-2 may function in a shared pathway to regulated pathogen avoidance behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that gon-2 and npr-15 mutants have similar avoidance phenotypes.

claim: GON-2 modulates avoidance behavior through the intestine.
source: As it has been previously demonstrated that GON-2 modulates avoidance behavior through the intestine (Filipowicz et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The inactivation of gon-2 in MGH171 and MGH171;npr-15(tm12539) exhibited comparable avoidance behaviors to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
source: Our results showed that the inactivation of gon-2 in MGH171 and MGH171;npr-15(tm12539) (Figure 5J), but not in TU3401 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), exhibited comparable avoidance behaviors to that of npr-15(tm12539) animals.
evidence: Supported by tissue-specific RNAi lawn occupancy data shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: NPR-15 acts through the intestinal TRPM channel GON-2 to control pathogen avoidance behavior.
source: These results suggest that NPR-15 acts through the intestinal TRPM channel GON-2 to control pathogen avoidance behavior.
evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific RNAi experiments showing intestinal requirement for GON-2 in avoidance.

claim: The avoidance behavior of ASJ(-);gon-2 is comparable to that of ASJ(-), ASJ(-);npr-15(tm12539), and gon-2 null animals when exposed to S. aureus.
source: Our results showed that the avoidance behavior of ASJ(-);gon-2 is comparable to that of ASJ(-), ASJ(-);npr-15(tm12539), and gon-2 null animals when exposed to S. aureus (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by lawn occupancy data with ASJ ablation and gon-2 RNAi shown in Figure 5K.

claim: NPR-15 controls S. aureus avoidance in a GON-2-dependent manner via the ASJ neuron.
source: These results suggest that NPR-15 controls S. aureus avoidance in a GON-2-dependent manner via the ASJ neuron.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments showing that ASJ and GON-2 are in the same pathway for avoidance.

claim: The neuronal GPCR/NPR-15 plays a dual role: suppressing the immune response and enhancing avoidance behavior toward S. aureus through sensory neurons, specifically ASJ.
source: In summary, the neuronal GPCR/NPR-15 plays a dual role: suppressing the immune response and enhancing avoidance behavior toward S. aureus through sensory neurons, specifically ASJ.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing NPR-15 controls both immunity and avoidance via ASJ neurons.

claim: The control of immunity against the pathogen S. aureus is dependent on the ELT-2 and HLH-30 transcription factors.
source: The control of immunity against the pathogen S. aureus is dependent on the ELT-2 and HLH-30 transcription factors, while the control of avoidance behavior is GON-2-dependent and mediated through the intestine (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments and summarized in Figure 6.

claim: The control of avoidance behavior is GON-2-dependent and mediated through the intestine.
source: The control of immunity against the pathogen S. aureus is dependent on the ELT-2 and HLH-30 transcription factors, while the control of avoidance behavior is GON-2-dependent and mediated through the intestine (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific RNAi experiments and summarized in Figure 6.

claim: GPCRs play a crucial role in neuronal and non-neuronal tissues in shaping both immune and avoidance behavioral responses toward invading pathogens.
source: GPCRs play a crucial role in neuronal and non-neuronal tissues in shaping both immune and avoidance behavioral responses toward invading pathogens (Furness and Sexton, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NPR-15 suppresses immune responses against different pathogen infections by inhibiting the activity of the GATA/ELT-2 and HLH-30 immune transcription regulators.
source: Our findings indicate that NPR-15 suppresses immune responses against different pathogen infections by inhibiting the activity of the GATA/ELT-2 and HLH-30 immune transcription regulators.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments showing ELT-2 and HLH-30 requirement for npr-15 phenotype.

claim: The control of the pathogen avoidance behavior by NPR-15 is independent of aerotaxis and dependent on intestinal GON-2.
source: Moreover, we found that the control of the pathogen avoidance behavior by NPR-15 is independent of aerotaxis and dependent on intestinal GON-2.
evidence: Inferred from oxygen manipulation experiments and tissue-specific RNAi experiments.

claim: NPR-15 controls the immunity-behavioral response via an amphid sensory neuron, ASJ, in response to S. aureus infection.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that NPR-15 controls the immunity-behavioral response via an amphid sensory neuron, ASJ, in response to S. aureus infection.
evidence: Inferred from neuron ablation and rescue experiments showing ASJ requirement.

claim: ASJ neurons are known to regulate different biological functions such as lifespan, dauer activities, head-directed light avoidance, and food search.
source: ASJ neurons are known to regulate different biological functions such as lifespan (Alcedo and Kenyon, 2004), dauer activities (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991; Chung et al., 2013), head-directed light avoidance (Ward et al., 2008), and food search (Macosko et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ASJ neurons play a role in the control of immune and behavioral responses against pathogen infection through GPCR/NPR-15.
source: We show here that ASJ neurons play a role in the control of immune and behavioral responses against pathogen infection through GPCR/NPR-15.
evidence: Inferred from neuron ablation and rescue experiments.

claim: The regulation of NPR-15-mediated avoidance is not influenced by intestinal immune and neuropeptide genes.
source: Our research additionally indicates that the regulation of NPR-15-mediated avoidance is not influenced by intestinal immune and neuropeptide genes.
evidence: Inferred from RNAi experiments showing that immune genes and neuropeptides do not affect avoidance.

claim: The octopamine receptor OCTR-1 functions in ASH/ASI neurons.
